supplement.where: Appendices A to D at the end of this PDF (pp. 32-34), cited in the main text (A and B on p. 10, C on p. 13, D on p. 16). The document names no separate online supplement. Data are on OSF: https://osf.io/nz6ag/?view_only=81c63168f1f64f62b2e865265b8ab343 (p. 8). On 2026-10-05 that OSF project held two files, CoCreativityDF.csv and AnalysisTable.docx. The paper does not cite either file by name.
supplement.holds: Appendices A and B: screenshots of the AI-help and No-AI writing interfaces. Appendix C: the prompt classification scheme. Appendix D: prompt-count correlations without outlier removal (t, r, p), which the main text lacks. No statistic for the AI-help vs No-AI contrasts sits only in the appendices. Those are all in the main text (pp. 14, 17, 18). Outside the PDF, CoCreativityDF.csv has 263 rows, one per analyzed participant, with each condition's originality, diversity contribution, word count, self-judgment, and self-judgment accuracy, three difference scores, integration, and the generation and elaboration prompt counts. It has no condition-order or prompt variable, no story texts, and no rows for the 128 removed people. AnalysisTable.docx lists every reported analysis with effect size, p value, and 95% CI. It prints the diversity contrast's CI as [-1.04, -0.006] with no scale label (the paper prints [-0.0001, -0.0000006]), and it gives the condition x self-assessment interaction as b = 0.001 with 95% CI [-.012, .01], a CI the paper lacks (the paper prints b = -0.001).

paper_design_summary: In an online study, each of 263 analyzed introductory psychology students at Pennsylvania State University (391 recruited, 128 removed after taking part) wrote two short stories of at least 150 words from a three-word prompt: one with a GPT-3.5 chatbot in a side box, limited by a hidden system prompt to bullet-point ideas (AI-help), and one without AI (No-AI). The order of the two conditions was randomized, and the two prompts were counterbalanced across conditions. Each story was scored for originality by an automated model (MAoSS) and for its contribution to the semantic diversity of all stories written to the same prompt (sentence embeddings), conditions were compared with paired t-tests, and participants also rated their own stories' originality.

studies.label: Within-subjects story writing with and without ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), randomized order

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two writing conditions (AI-help first or No-AI first). Every participant wrote one story in each condition. The two three-word prompts (pen-paper-write, year-week-embark) were counterbalanced across conditions; the paper does not say how.
assignment.quote: Participants completed two stories, with (AI-help) and without AI help (No-AI). The order of presentation was randomized, such that an equal number of participants completed the AI-help and No-AI conditions first.
assignment.locator: p. 9, Method, Story Writing Task; the within-subjects design is also stated on p. 8, The Present Research

arms.name: AI-help
arms.description: Story written while the participant could chat freely with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 through a custom API) in a side text box. A hidden system prompt framed the model as a creativity support tool, limited its output to bullet points, and prevented full story passages. Copy-paste was disabled site-wide, and participants were told to use ChatGPT only as a 'source of ideas'.

arms.name: No-AI
arms.description: Story written in a matched interface with the ChatGPT text box removed, so only the story box showed (Appendix B). During the practice task, participants were told to pose the suggested prompting strategies to themselves as brainstorming when writing without ChatGPT. Before either condition, every participant completed a practice story structured like the AI-help condition, with ChatGPT available. The paper does not say whether each participant sent ChatGPT a message in the practice.

participants.exclusions: 391 students recruited for the online study. Removed from the sample using responses collected in the study: 68 who reported using external aid such as AI or the internet (beyond the AI provided in the experiment), 53 who failed either of two attention checks in the questionnaire portion that followed the story task, and 7 who scored below 2.5 SD on any intelligence test. 391 - 68 - 53 - 7 = 263 analyzed. The removed people took part, so they were dropped after participation. c475, which reanalyzes these participants, says the intelligence tasks came after the story writing (c475 p. 6). The paper gives no count at assignment or by order, and its statement that an equal number did each order first cannot be exact for 391 or 263, since both are odd. Each of the 263 analyzed participants contributes one story to each arm, and both paired t-tests have df = 262. The text says the prompt-count correlations drop a further 2 (generation) and 7 (elaboration) outliers above 3 SD (p. 16). The dfs conflict for generation count: t(254) and the partial t(253) for originality vs generation count imply 256 people (7 removed), while t(259) for diversity vs generation count fits 261 (2 removed) (pp. 16-17). These correlations are not coded outcomes.
participants.who: Students enrolled in an introductory psychology course at Pennsylvania State University. 235 female, 27 male, 3 other (these sum to 265, not the stated 263). Mean age 18.9 (SD 2.17). 74 percent Caucasian. 95 percent had used ChatGPT or another LLM chatbot before.
participants.quote: In total, our final sample consisted of 263 participants (235 female, 27 male, 3 other; mean age = 18.9 years, SD = 2.17).

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT based on the GPT-3.5 base model, called through a custom API with a hidden system prompt
ai_tool.how_used: Participants typed free messages to ChatGPT in one text box while writing the story in another. A hidden system prompt, entered before any exchange, framed the model as a creativity support tool and limited its output to bullet points so that it would not write story passages. Copy-paste was disabled across the website, and participants were told not to ask ChatGPT to write the story but to use it as a 'source of ideas'. Before either condition, every participant completed a practice story (50 words minimum, 2 minutes recommended) structured like the AI-help condition, with suggested prompting strategies.

task.description: Short story of at least 150 words that uses all three words of a prompt (pen-paper-write or year-week-embark), adapted from the five-sentence short-story task. Participants were told to 'use their imagination and be creative'. The interface screenshots (Appendices A and B) also show an on-screen request for a 'very short story (~5 sentences long)'.
task.duration: Instructed to spend at least 10 minutes per story (not enforced); submission blocked until the story reached 150 words.

outcomes.name: Story originality (MAoSS score)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Multilingual Assessment of Short Stories (MAoSS), a fine-tuned LLM on the Creativity Assessment Platform trained to predict human-rated originality. Its predictions correlate with human ratings of English stories at r = .86 (p. 11). Scale 0-1 (p. 18). No robustness variant of the arm contrast is reported. Partial correlations controlling for the word-count difference appear only in the correlational analyses of engagement with the AI (pp. 15-17).

contrasts.reported: Paired-samples t-test: AI-help M = .56, SD = 08 vs No-AI M = .52, SD = 08 (both SDs printed without a decimal point); t(262) = 5.56, p < .001, d = .34, 95% CI [.021, .045]. n = 263 analyzed in each condition (within person). The paper does not say what the CI bounds or which SD d uses.
contrasts.locator: p. 14, Results, Story Originality; Figure 2 (left panel), p. 15

outcomes.name: Diversity contribution of each story
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Leave-one-out contribution of each story to the diversity of its prompt dataset: dataset diversity (mean pairwise semantic distance, 1 - cosine, between sentence embeddings) minus the same mean with the story removed. Positive = the story adds diversity. Prompt words were removed before embedding. Figure 2 plots the values multiplied by 10^3. No robustness variant of the arm contrast is reported.

contrasts.reported: Paired-samples t-test: AI-help M = -.000026, SD = .00033 vs No-AI M = .000027, SD = .00034; t(262) = -1.99, p = .047, d = -.123, 95% CI [-0.0001, -0.0000006]. n = 263 analyzed in each condition (within person). Higher = more diverse, so no sign reversal is needed: AI-help stories contributed less diversity.
contrasts.locator: p. 17, Results, Story Diversity; Figure 2 (middle panel, values x 10^3), p. 15

diversity_detail.metric: Per-story leave-one-out diversity contribution: mean pairwise semantic distance (1 - cosine) over all story pairs in the prompt dataset minus the same mean with the story removed
diversity_detail.embedding_model: paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 (SentenceTransformers), embeddings from the final layer (layer 12)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of stories within each of two datasets defined by the three-word prompt (pen-paper-write, year-week-embark), with prompt words removed. The datasets are split by prompt only. Since prompts were counterbalanced across conditions (p. 9), each dataset holds both AI-help and No-AI stories, although the paper does not say so directly. Each score is therefore a story's contribution to a mixed pool, not to its own arm's pool.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Paired-samples t-test across the 263 analyzed participants, each contributing one AI-help and one No-AI score (df = 262).
diversity_detail.notes: Arm-level set diversity (mean pairwise distance within each arm) is not reported. Diversity difference scores (AI-help minus No-AI) were unrelated to AI-response integration and to generation and elaboration prompt counts (p. 17). The authors note that the effect is smaller than in Doshi and Hauser (2024) and that the measure needs validation (p. 22).

outcomes.name: Self-assessed originality and its accuracy
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: At the end of the story task, each participant rated the originality of each own story from 1 (Not at all original) to 5 (Very original) (p. 11). The paper analyzes accuracy three ways: Kendall's tau between self-ratings and MAoSS in each condition; a multilevel model (lme4) with participant random intercepts that tests the condition x self-assessment interaction on MAoSS, with one row per self-rated story; and an error score (self-rating minus MAoSS min-max rescaled to 1-5). It is a self-report, so it does not satisfy criterion 3 and answers none of the three questions.

contrasts.reported: Kendall's tau between self-assessment and MAoSS: AI-help 0.161, p < .001, 95% CI [.078, .244]; No-AI 0.195, p < .001, 95% CI [.112, .278]. Condition x self-assessment interaction on MAoSS: t(413) = -0.22, p = .83, b = -0.001 (no SE printed). Self-assessment error: AI-help M = 2.43, SD = 1.15; No-AI M = 2.14, SD = 1.18 (no test printed).
contrasts.locator: pp. 17-18, Results, Self-Assessment Accuracy; Figure 2 (right panel), p. 15

eligibility.reason: Within-person design: every participant wrote one story with and one without ChatGPT, and the order of conditions was randomized (p. 9), which the codebook accepts. 263 people were analyzed (p. 9), and both paired t-tests have df = 262 (pp. 14 and 17). Originality is scored on each story by the MAoSS model (p. 11), and diversity contribution by sentence embeddings of the stories (pp. 11-12). Of the two scored stories, ChatGPT was available only for the AI-help story (p. 10). The abstract's 'naturalistic study' refers to free interaction with ChatGPT (p. 19), not to non-random assignment. Caveats: every participant completed a practice story with ChatGPT available before both conditions (p. 10), 128 people were removed after participation, and the paper gives no counts by order.

one_line_finding: Within person, stories written with GPT-3.5 available scored higher on MAoSS originality (M = .56 vs .52; t(262) = 5.56, p < .001, d = .34; p. 14) and contributed less to semantic diversity (t(262) = -1.99, p = .047, d = -.123; p. 17) than the same 263 analyzed students' stories written without AI (Figure 2, p. 15).
open_questions: Carryover: before both conditions, every participant completed a practice story with ChatGPT available, structured like the AI-help condition (p. 10), and about half wrote the No-AI story after the AI-help story (p. 9). The paper does not say whether each participant sent ChatGPT a message in the practice, and it reports no order or carryover analysis. So no No-AI story was written before exposure to the ChatGPT interface, and no after_ai estimate is given. The posted CSV has no order variable.

Exclusions remove a person from both arms, but the paper does not report the 128 removals (including 68 for self-reported external aid) by order, nor how many of the 391 began with each condition. It cannot be checked whether removal depended on the order of conditions. The posted CSV holds only the 263 analyzed participants.

Diversity contribution is computed within prompt datasets that pool both conditions, not within each condition's set of stories, and no arm-level set diversity is reported (pp. 11-12). Whether it serves as the across_people measure under codebook section 8, rule 2, needs a decision. A within-arm measure would need the story texts, which are not posted.

The paper does not say what the 95% CIs bound or which SD d uses. Arithmetic check for the extraction phase: the CI midpoints match the raw mean differences (.033, and -.0000503 vs -.000053 from the printed means), and the printed d values equal t / sqrt(263) (.343, -.123). This is consistent with d standardized by the SD of paired differences, not by an arm SD (codebook section 9).

The originality SDs are printed as 'SD = 08' (p. 14) without a decimal point. They are recorded as printed. Extraction should confirm the value from the posted CSV, which holds both originality scores for each of the 263 analyzed participants.

The gender counts (235 + 27 + 3 = 265) do not sum to the stated final sample of 263 (p. 9). The exclusion arithmetic (391 - 68 - 53 - 7 = 263), df = 262, and the 263 rows of the posted CSV support 263 analyzed.

Prompt-count outliers: the text says 2 generation and 7 elaboration outliers were removed (p. 16). For originality vs generation count, t(254) and the partial t(253) imply 256 people (7 removed), but the printed 95% CI [.072, .306] matches a Fisher-z interval for 261 people (2 removed, r taken from the printed t), and diversity vs generation count has t(259) (p. 17). The printed CI for diversity vs generation count, [-.198, .042], matches the Appendix D analysis without outlier removal (t(261) = -1.28, r = -.08), not the printed t(259) = -0.55. The source does not settle which number is the misprint. These correlations are not coded outcomes, and the posted CSV holds the prompt counts and difference scores needed to rerun them.
notes: PDF pages carry no printed page numbers; locators use PDF page order. The markdown conversion holds the full text through Appendix D but omits Figures 1-3 and the Appendix A and B screenshots, which were read from the PDF. Self-assessment accuracy is kept as S1-O3 (self-report, question none) and does not affect eligibility. Not listed as outcomes: correlations of within-person originality and diversity difference scores with the integration of AI responses and with generation and elaboration prompt counts (pp. 14-17, Figure 3, Appendix D). They are not contrasts between assigned conditions, and those measures exist only in the AI-help condition. No condition contrast on word count is reported; word count enters only as a control in those correlations. A battery of classical creativity tasks preceded the story task and questionnaires followed it. The paper calls them not relevant to its research questions (p. 9) and names no other paper using these participants. Study 1 of c475 (Luchini, Kaufman and Beaty 2025, posted later) reanalyzes them, so the c475 record should carry the same sample_id (see sample_overlap). c475 names the tool 'ChatGPT-3.5-Turbo (accessed February 2025)' (c475 p. 7); this form keeps c159's own wording. Appendix D's third and fourth lines carry the same label ('Diversity Difference Score ~ Generation Prompt Count') with different statistics (p. 34), so one label is a typo. Design class online_rct: an unsupervised online study (Qualtrics plus a custom website) with a course participant pool, not a supervised session. Structure is coded within, following the paper's term 'within-subjects design' (p. 8); it is a two-period design with randomized order. This file replaces an earlier reconciliation (written 9:20 AM on 2026-10-05) that was based on earlier versions of the two raw forms. Finalized on 2026-10-05 after the assignment, people, and outcome challenges (see final.challenge_resolution).

challenge_resolution.problem: arms[No-AI].description, eligibility.reason, and open_questions[0] said every participant had used ChatGPT in the practice story. The paper says only that everyone completed a practice task structured like the AI-help condition, as an opportunity to get familiar with LLM prompting.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: The three fields now say that every participant completed a practice story with ChatGPT available before either condition, and that the paper does not say whether each participant sent ChatGPT a message. The AI-help screen sets no minimum ('send as many messages as you need to complete your story', Appendix A, p. 32), and Figure 3 (left panel, p. 16) plots a column of participants at an integration score of 0.0. Criterion 1 is unaffected. The reconciliation object keeps its earlier wording in agreed_fields_checked, because it is left unchanged.

challenge_resolution.problem: participants.exclusions recorded 2 generation and 7 elaboration prompt-count outliers without noting that t(254) and the partial t(253) for originality vs generation count imply 256 people (7 removed), while t(259) for diversity vs generation count fits 261 (2 removed).
challenge_resolution.what_changed: participants.exclusions and a new open question now record the conflict. The checker's inference that 7, not 2, generation outliers were removed is not adopted, because the source does not settle it. The text says 2, t(259) for diversity fits 2, and the printed 95% CI [.072, .306] for originality vs generation count matches a Fisher-z interval for 261 people, not for 256 ([.073, .309]), with r taken from the printed t. The same computation reproduces the printed CIs of the n = 263 correlations on pp. 15-16. Only t(254) and t(253) imply 7. These correlations are not coded outcomes, so no count, outcome, or criterion changes.
challenge_resolution.quote: In this way, we removed 2 data points for our generative prompt count analysis, and 7 data points for our elaboration prompt count analysis.
challenge_resolution.locator: p. 16, Results, Story Originality (removal sentence at the top; t(254) and t(253) for generation count below it); p. 17, Results, Story Diversity (t(259))

open_items.item: Carryover: every participant completed a practice story with ChatGPT available before both conditions, about half wrote the No-AI story second, and the paper reports no order or carryover analysis (pp. 9-10). The posted CSV has no order variable.

Removals by order: the paper gives no count at assignment or by order for the 128 people removed, and 'an equal number' doing each order first cannot be exact for 391 or 263 (pp. 8-9). The posted CSV holds only the 263 analyzed. Criterion 1 rests on the stated randomized order, and each removal drops a person from both arms.

Diversity contribution is measured against prompt pools that mix both arms, and no arm-level set diversity is reported (pp. 11-12). Whether it can be the across_people primary record (codebook section 8, rule 2) is a Review 1 coding decision, not missing information. Criterion 3 holds through S1-O1 alone. A within-arm measure would need the story texts, which are not posted.

The paper does not say what its 95% CIs bound or which SD d uses (pp. 14, 17). The printed numbers already show CI midpoints equal to the mean differences and d = t / sqrt(263), consistent with d standardized by the SD of paired differences.
Originality SDs printed as 'SD = 08' without a decimal point (p. 14). The posted CSV holds both originality scores for all 263 analyzed participants.
Gender counts sum to 265, not the stated 263 (p. 9). The analyzed count of 263 is fixed by the exclusion arithmetic, df = 262, and the 263 posted rows, and either count is far above 50.

Prompt-count outliers: the text says 2 generation outliers were removed, but t(254) and t(253) for originality vs generation count imply 7 (pp. 16-17). Not a coded outcome. The posted CSV holds the prompt counts and difference scores to rerun the correlations.
